title: Monolith vs Microservices
summary: What actually changes when you split a monolith into services, and a framework for deciding when that trade-off is worth taking.

slides.markdown:
A **monolith** is one deployable unit running your whole application; **microservices** split that unit into many independently deployable services that talk over the network. Neither is inherently better — the split trades simplicity for independent scaling, deployment, and failure isolation.

Think of it like a single restaurant kitchen versus a food court: one kitchen is simpler to run, but a food court lets each stall scale, change its menu, and fail without shutting down the others.

slides.sectionTitle: What a monolith actually is (and why it isn't as bad as its reputation)
slides.markdown:
A **monolith** is a single codebase, single build, single deployable artifact — one process (or one horizontally-scaled fleet of identical processes) serving every feature. It usually shares one database.

The reputation problem: "monolith" gets used as a synonym for "legacy mess," but the two are separate axes. A **modular monolith** — one deployable, but internally split into clean packages with enforced boundaries — gives you most of the maintainability benefits people credit to microservices, without any network calls. Stack Overflow and Shopify's core run this way at massive scale.

The real question isn't "monolith or not" — it's whether your team needs *independent deployability* badly enough to pay for the network boundary.

slides.sectionTitle: What "microservices" changes: deployment, ownership, failure isolation
slides.markdown:
Splitting into microservices changes three things at once, not just "where the code lives."

**Deployment** — each service ships on its own schedule; a bug fix to checkout no longer requires redeploying search. **Ownership** — a team can own a service end-to-end (code, data, on-call) instead of everyone sharing one codebase. **Failure isolation** — if the recommendations service crashes, checkout can keep running (if you've designed for it) instead of taking the whole process down.

None of this is free: you now need service discovery, network retries, and distributed debugging where a single stack trace used to suffice.

![Monolith with one database vs microservices each with their own](assets/monolith-vs-microservices.svg)

The monolith has one deployment unit and one database; the microservices version has independently deployed services, each usually owning its own data store, calling each other over the network instead of via in-process function calls.

The topology shift is what introduces every microservices problem covered later in this group: discovery, partial failure, and data consistency across services.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: monolith vs microservices on velocity, complexity, operational cost
slides.markdown:
| | Monolith | Microservices |
|---|---|---|
| Early velocity | Fast — one codebase, one deploy, no network to design around | Slower — must design APIs, ownership, and infra before writing much logic |
| Velocity at scale (many teams) | Slows — one deploy pipeline, one release train, merge conflicts | Faster — teams ship independently once boundaries are stable |
| Operational complexity | Low — one thing to monitor, deploy, and roll back | High — dozens of deployables, network calls, distributed tracing |
| Failure blast radius | Whole app can go down together | Can be contained to one service, if designed for it |

**How to decide:** if you have one team and a codebase that fits in a few people's heads, the monolith's simplicity wins; the trade flips once enough independent teams need to ship on their own schedule without blocking each other.

slides.sectionTitle: The organizational reason for microservices (Conway's Law)
slides.markdown:
**Conway's Law**: organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. If you have four teams, you'll tend to end up with a system that has roughly four major seams, whether you plan it that way or not.

This is why microservices are as much an organizational decision as a technical one: splitting services along team boundaries lets each team ship without coordinating a joint release with three other teams. Splitting services *against* team boundaries — one team owning code that spans three services — recreates the monolith's coordination cost, just with extra network latency added on top.

If you're proposing microservices in an interview, naming the team structure they'd map to is a strong signal.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adopting microservices for a team too small to operate them
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Netflix and Amazon use microservices, so we should too — it's the modern, scalable way to build."

**Why it's wrong:** microservices add a fixed operational tax — service discovery, distributed tracing, per-service CI/CD, on-call for each deployable — that a 5-engineer team pays in full for a fraction of the benefit. A team that size can't staff separate on-call rotations per service, so an outage means the same few people debugging across a dozen network hops instead of one process.

**Correct model:** adopt microservices when the *coordination cost* of a shared monolith (multiple teams blocking each other's releases) exceeds the *operational cost* of running distributed infrastructure — not because a larger company's architecture looks impressive.
